newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish navy to flex muscles in Cyprus.
newsitem.headline: Turkish navy to flex muscles in Cyprus.

text.p: Turkish navy vessels are to visit northern Cyprus this week as part of a wide-ranging show of solidarity with the breakaway Turkish Cypriot state, Turkey's military chief said on Tuesday.

"Our navy ships are going to the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus on January 24," Anatolian news agency quoted General Ismail Hakki Karadayi as saying before talks with visiting Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash.
A military official told Reuters the ships were likely to be a frigate and two assault boats.
Turkey has promised closer military and political links with the Turkish Cypriots in response to Greek Cypriot plans to install anti-aircraft missiles from Russia on the south of the island.
Turkey, which has around 30,000 soldiers on Cyprus, has threatened to use force to halt the deployment of the S-300 missiles. They are due to be installed in 16 months.
"We are not going to wait about passively for these 16 months," Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan told a meeting of his Islam-based Welfare Party.
He called on the Greek Cypriot administration, regarded internationally as the island's only government, to announce it will scrap the missile deal.
Cyprus has been divided since Turkey invaded in 1974 in response to a Greek Cypriot coup backed by Athens.
Denktash called on Turkey to push the cause of the Turkish Cypriots in the international arena as a matter of human rights.
"Come together and let's tell (foreign) parliamentarians about this human rights issue," he said in a speech to the Turkish parliament.
Parliament issued a declaration condemning both the Greek Cypriot missile deal as a threat to Turkey and "the embargo" on Turkish Cypriots.
The self-declared Turkish Cypriot state is recognised only by Ankara and is struggling under a European Union trade ban.
The declaration said Ankara would maintain economic support for the ailing Turkish Cypriot economy, to which it recently granted credit worth $250 million for economic reforms.
